introduction.heading: Doing More Than One Thing at a Time
introduction.description: A thread is an independent path of execution inside a running program. Every Java program starts with one - the `main` thread - but it can start more, and the JVM (with the operating system) interleaves them so several things appear to happen at once, or genuinely do on a multi-core CPU. Each thread gets its own call stack, but all threads in the program share the same heap. That single fact explains both why threads are useful (they can cooperate on shared data) and why they are dangerous (two threads touching the same object at the same instant can corrupt it). Spring Boot makes this unavoidable: every incoming HTTP request is handled on a thread from a pool, and your singleton beans are used by many of them at once.

concepts.title: Each Thread Has Its Own Stack, All Share One Heap
concepts.description: A thread's local variables and method frames live on its private stack, so they can never be seen by another thread. Objects on the heap are reachable from every thread that holds a reference - which is exactly where the sharing, and the trouble, comes from

concepts.title: start() vs run()
concepts.description: `thread.start()` asks the JVM to create a new thread that then calls `run()`. Calling `run()` yourself is just an ordinary method call on the current thread - nothing concurrent happens. Calling `start()` twice on the same Thread throws an exception

concepts.title: Runnable and Callable
concepts.description: A `Runnable` is a task with no return value and no checked exceptions; a `Callable<T>` returns a result and may throw. Both describe the work; a Thread or an executor decides where and when it runs. Because both are functional interfaces, a lambda is usually all you need

concepts.title: The Thread Lifecycle
concepts.description: A thread is NEW until `start()`, then RUNNABLE (running or ready to run). It can be BLOCKED waiting for a lock, WAITING or TIMED_WAITING (`wait`, `join`, `sleep`), and finally TERMINATED when `run()` returns or throws. Knowing the state is half of reading a thread dump

concepts.title: Race Conditions
concepts.description: When the outcome depends on how two threads happen to interleave, you have a race condition. `count++` looks like one step but is three - read, add, write - so two threads can both read the same old value and one update is silently lost. The bug is intermittent, which makes it hard to find and easy to ship

concepts.title: synchronized, Locks, and Atomics
concepts.description: `synchronized` lets only one thread at a time hold an object's monitor, turning a block into an indivisible unit. `ReentrantLock` offers the same with more control. `AtomicInteger` and friends do single-variable updates safely without locking. `volatile` guarantees visibility of a write across threads, but not atomicity of `count++`

concepts.title: Executors and Thread Pools
concepts.description: Creating a thread per task is expensive and unbounded. An `ExecutorService` keeps a fixed set of worker threads and queues tasks for them. You `submit` work, get a `Future` back, and call `shutdown()` when you are done. Prefer this over creating `Thread` objects by hand

concepts.title: Futures and CompletableFuture
concepts.description: `Future.get()` blocks until the result is ready. `CompletableFuture` lets you chain steps (`thenApply`, `thenCombine`) and run several asynchronous calls in parallel, then combine their results without blocking a thread in between

concepts.title: Deadlock
concepts.description: Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1 - neither can ever proceed. The standard defence is to always acquire multiple locks in the same global order, or to avoid holding more than one at all

concepts.title: Thread-Safe Collections and Immutability
concepts.description: `ArrayList` and `HashMap` are not safe to modify from several threads. Use `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList` or the other `java.util.concurrent` collections. Immutable objects (final fields, no setters) need no locking at all, which is the cheapest way to be thread-safe

interleaving.heading: Watching Two Threads Collide
interleaving.description: Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter that starts at 0, so the answer should be 2. Step through an unlucky interleaving of the unsafe version, then switch to the synchronized version and see how the lock forces the threads to take turns.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Before reaching for threads, ask whether you need them: a plain loop or a stream is simpler, and `parallelStream()` only pays off for large, CPU-heavy, independent work
Prefer an `ExecutorService` (or, on Java 21+, virtual threads via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`) over `new Thread(...)` - and always `shutdown()` the pool, or the JVM will not exit
Ask of every field: can two threads touch this at once? If yes and it is mutable, it needs a lock, an atomic type, or a thread-safe collection - or should be made immutable
Keep `synchronized` blocks as small as you can, never call unknown code while holding a lock, and always take multiple locks in the same order
Never rely on a test passing once as proof of thread safety - races are timing-dependent. Reason about shared state instead, and use `join()` or `Future.get()` before reading results
In Spring, treat every singleton bean as shared between threads: no mutable instance fields for per-request data - keep that in method parameters and local variables

practiceTopics.title: Thread States
practiceTopics.description: Match each situation - after start(), waiting on a lock, inside sleep(), after run() returns - to the thread state the JVM reports

practiceTopics.title: Predict the Output: Threads
practiceTopics.description: Short snippets about start() versus run(), unsynchronized counters, atomics, and join() - predict what actually happens

practiceTopics.title: Thread Pool Scheduler
practiceTopics.description: Pick a pool size and watch six tasks of different lengths get assigned to worker threads on a timeline - see why more workers help, and where they stop helping

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A broken counter, a fixed counter, and a thread pool
fullExample.description: Two threads hammer the same pair of counters 1000 times each - one unsafe, one atomic - and then a fixed pool of three workers processes five orders. Run it a few times: the unsafe total changes from run to run, the safe one never does.

steps.label: Shared objects and a task to run
steps.explanation: `unsafe` and `safe` are heap objects, and the `work` lambda captures references to both. Whichever thread runs `work` increments the very same two objects - that is the sharing. `work` itself is just a `Runnable`: a description of a task, not a thread.

steps.label: start() and join()
steps.explanation: Each `new Thread(work)` only creates the thread object; nothing runs until `start()`. From that point `t1`, `t2` and `main` all run concurrently, in no guaranteed order. `join()` makes `main` wait until the thread has finished - without it, `main` could read the counters while the work is still going on.

steps.label: The results
steps.explanation: Two threads times 1000 increments should give exactly 2000. The safe counter always does. The unsafe one usually prints something slightly lower, and a different number on each run - the signature of a race condition.

steps.label: A fixed thread pool and Futures
steps.explanation: `newFixedThreadPool(3)` creates three reusable workers; `submit` queues each of the five tasks and immediately returns a `Future`. `f.get()` blocks until that task's result is ready. Five tasks never need five threads - the pool reuses its three. `shutdown()` lets the workers finish and then exit; forgetting it keeps the JVM alive.

steps.label: UnsafeCounter: count++ is not atomic
steps.explanation: `count++` compiles to read, add one, write back. If two threads both read 41 before either writes, both write 42 and one increment vanishes. The method looks harmless precisely because the bug is not on any single line.

steps.label: SafeCounter: an atomic update
steps.explanation: `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` performs the read-modify-write as one indivisible operation using a CPU-level compare-and-set, so no update can be lost and no lock is needed. Declaring the field `final` is still good practice - the reference never changes, only the value inside.

quiz.question: What happens if you call `thread.run()` instead of `thread.start()`?
options: A new thread is created and runs the task - the two are equivalent
The task runs as an ordinary method call on the current thread, with no concurrency
A compile error occurs
The task is queued and runs later on the main thread
quiz.explanation: Only `start()` asks the JVM to create a new thread. `run()` is just the method the new thread would have called - invoking it directly runs it right here, to completion, before the next line.

quiz.question: Two threads each execute `count++` 1000 times on the same plain `int` field. What can the final value be?
options: Always exactly 2000
Often less than 2000 and different on each run, because increments can be lost
Always exactly 1000
It throws a ConcurrentModificationException
quiz.explanation: `count++` is read-add-write. When two threads interleave between the read and the write, one update overwrites the other. The result is usually a bit under 2000 and different every run.

quiz.question: Which data does one thread NOT share with another thread in the same program?
options: Objects on the heap that both hold a reference to
Static fields
The local variables in its own method frames
Fields of a singleton Spring bean
quiz.explanation: Each thread has a private call stack, so its local variables and parameters are invisible to other threads. Heap objects and static fields are shared, which is why those need protection.

quiz.question: Why is `volatile int count` not enough to make `count++` thread-safe?
options: volatile does nothing at all
volatile makes writes visible to other threads, but the read-add-write is still three separate steps that can interleave
volatile only works on objects, not primitives
volatile makes the field read-only
quiz.explanation: `volatile` guarantees visibility and ordering, not atomicity. Use `AtomicInteger` or a `synchronized` block when an update depends on the current value.

quiz.question: Why use an `ExecutorService` instead of creating a new Thread for every task?
options: Threads created with `new Thread` cannot run Runnables
A pool reuses a bounded number of worker threads, avoiding the cost and unbounded growth of one thread per task, and gives you Futures
Executors make code run on the GPU
It removes the need for any synchronization
quiz.explanation: Thread creation is costly and unlimited threads exhaust memory. A pool reuses workers and queues extra work. It does not remove the need to protect shared mutable state.

quiz.question: Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y; thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. What is this?
options: A race condition
A deadlock
A memory leak
Normal behaviour that resolves itself after a timeout
quiz.explanation: Each thread is waiting for something only the other can release, so neither ever proceeds. Acquiring locks in a consistent global order prevents it.
